title: Chain of Responsibility Pattern
summary: Passing a request along a chain of handlers until one of them handles it — the shape behind HTTP middleware, validation pipelines, and exception-handler chains.

slides.markdown:
**Chain of Responsibility** passes a request through a sequence of handlers, each deciding whether to handle it, pass it along, or both. An HTTP request hits an auth check, then a rate limiter, then your actual route handler — each one is independent and doesn't know or care what comes before or after it.

The sender of the request only knows about the first handler in the chain; it has no idea how many handlers exist or which one will end up acting on it.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: a request that might be handled by one of several possible handlers
slides.markdown:
An incoming HTTP request might need authentication, rate limiting, and request-body validation before it ever reaches business logic — and which checks apply can vary by route. The naive fix is one function that checks `isAuthenticated()`, then `isWithinRateLimit()`, then `isValidBody()`, all inline, in order.

That function becomes a chokepoint: every route needs slightly different checks in a different order, and the function keeps growing new `if` branches and parameters to configure which checks apply where. Adding a new check (say, IP allow-listing) means editing this one function and re-testing every route that flows through it.

The underlying problem: a request might need to pass through zero or more of several independent checks, and hardcoding the exact sequence into one function couples all of them together and makes each route's specific combination hard to express.

slides.sectionTitle: Chain of Responsibility: pass the request along a chain until someone handles it
slides.markdown:
Each check becomes its own **handler** object implementing one method, say `handle(request)`, and holding a reference to the *next* handler in the chain. A handler does its own check, and then either short-circuits (rejects the request, stops the chain) or calls `next.handle(request)` to pass it along.

The chain is assembled once — `auth.setNext(rateLimiter); rateLimiter.setNext(validator);` — and the caller only ever calls `auth.handle(request)`, the first link. Each handler is single-purpose, independently testable, and completely unaware of how many handlers come after it or what they do.

Reordering or adding a check means changing how the chain is *assembled*, not editing any individual handler's code.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a request traveling handler to handler
slides.markdown:
A request enters at the first handler. Each handler either stops it (handles or rejects it) or forwards it unchanged to the next link. No handler knows the chain's total length or what's further down it — only its own immediate `next` reference.

<<< Image: a request arrow entering a row of three handler boxes in sequence (AuthHandler, RateLimitHandler, BusinessLogicHandler), each with an arrow to the next labeled 'pass along', and a dashed arrow from each box labeled 'reject/short-circuit' exiting downward >>>

The request itself doesn't change shape as it moves — what changes is which handler currently has the option to act on it.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a middleware/validation chain — auth to rate-limit to business logic
Compare: Chain of Responsibility vs a single handler with if/else branches
slides.markdown:
| | Chain of Responsibility | Single handler with if/else |
|---|---|---|
| Adding a new check | New handler class, wire it into the chain | Add another branch to the existing function |
| Reordering checks | Reassign `setNext()` calls | Reorder branches, re-verify the whole function |
| Reusing checks across different flows | Compose different chains from the same handler classes | Duplicate the relevant branches into a new function |
| Overhead for 1-2 checks that never change | Extra classes and wiring for little benefit | Simple, direct, easy to read |

**How to decide:** for a small, stable set of checks always applied in the same order, one function is perfectly fine. Reach for Chain of Responsibility once different call sites need different subsets or orderings of the same checks.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a chain with no handler at the end, silently swallowing the request
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If no handler in the chain explicitly rejects the request, it must have been handled correctly."

**Why it's wrong:** if the last handler in the chain calls `next.handle(request)` and `next` is `undefined` — because whoever assembled the chain forgot to terminate it — the request can silently fall off the end with no response ever sent, no error thrown, and no log entry. The caller just hangs or times out, and debugging "why did this request vanish" is painful precisely because nothing failed loudly.

**Correct model:** every chain needs an explicit terminal handler — a default that always responds (even if just a 404 or "unhandled") rather than assuming the chain naturally has an end. Treat "no handler took this" as a case to handle explicitly, not an impossible state.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up: HTTP middleware, exception-handler chains, logging levels
slides.markdown:
**HTTP middleware** in frameworks like Express, Django, or ASP.NET is Chain of Responsibility by name in some ecosystems and by shape in all of them — each middleware function decides to act, modify the request, or call `next()`. **Exception handling** in languages with a catch-chain (a `try` with multiple `catch` blocks, or a chain of exception handlers each checking if it handles a particular error type) is the same shape applied to errors instead of requests.

**Logging frameworks** with severity levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR) that pass a log message up a chain of appenders, each deciding whether its configured level cares about this message, is a classic real-world instance — a message not consumed by the DEBUG appender still continues to the ERROR appender, exactly like an unhandled request moving to the next link.
